To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the gold–alkynide bond in gold–alkyne complexes is stronger than the known multiple gold–carbon bonds, that the gold–ligand bond strength is inversely correlated with bond order, and that the gold–carbide bond strength is enhanced for more electronegtive ligands.

the gold–ligand bond in the Cl Au–CCH− is the strongest gold–carbon bond known, that the gold–C bond strength is correlated with the ligand’s electronegativity, and that the strong gold–ligand bonding is a prerequisite for catalytic activity.
gold(I)–CCH− is the strongest gold–carbon single bond, and the gold(I)–carbon bond in alkynyl complexes depends on the ancillary gold ligands.

the nature of the metal–carbon bond in gold(I) complexes and how this bond influences the reactivity of gold catalysts.
the fundamental understanding of the nature of the gold–ligand bonding and its implications to the catalysis by gold.
the development of novel gold(I)– and gold(III)–catalysed C–C and C–N bond-forming reactions.

the nature of the gold–C bond in the alkynyl–Au(I) complexes is not a single bond, but rather it is a bond of intermediate character between a single and a double bond.

we have shown that gold can form very strong bonds to carbon, even stronger than multiple bonds.
gold(I)–carbon multiple bonds are stronger than expected, and the strength of the gold–alkynide bond depends on the ligands.

the gold–alkynide bond is a unique gold–carbon bond, distinct from the gold–alkyne bond and the gold–alkyl bond.
